summary: Defines the Robust Header Compression framework, a way to shrink packet headers efficiently over links with different characteristics. It separates the framework and the profile for uncompressed packets from the original definition in RFC 3095. It is a proposed standard that replaced RFC 4995.

plainLanguage.summary: ROHC is the rulebook for making packet headers smaller on a link. It works by sending the parts of a header that never change only once, and then sending only what changed. Each end keeps a note of what it has already sent, so a lost packet is noticed rather than silently corrupting everything after it.

subtitle: The common rulebook for squeezing IP, UDP, RTP and TCP headers over links that lose and corrupt packets.

tldr.problem: On a slow or expensive link, the repeated part of every packet header is a large share of the traffic, and a scheme that assumes nothing is ever lost cannot take that saving.
tldr.mechanism: ROHC splits the header into fields by how they change, sends the constant parts once, and keeps a context at each end. Every compressed packet carries a checksum, so a receiver that rebuilds a header wrongly can notice and ask for a repair.
tldr.outcome: Headers can be cut to a few octet on lossy links without a lost packet causing every later packet to fail. This document separates the framework from the profiles, and adds the profile that does not compress at all. It replaced RFC 4995 in 2010.

today: RFC 5795 is a Proposed Standard on the IETF Standards Track. It replaced RFC 4995 in 2010, fixing one interoperability issue that RFC 4995 had introduced in the reading of the Size field in ROHC feedback, and it has not itself been obsoleted or updated. It separates the framework from the profiles, and adds the uncompressed profile 0x0000; the framework itself is unchanged from RFC 3095.

sections.title: What Header Compression Is For
sections.content:
For many kinds of network, reducing deployment and operating costs by using the available bandwidth well is of vital importance. Header compression over a link is possible because some of the information carried in a packet header becomes redundant from packet to packet.

The redundancy is there between consecutive packets of the same flow. End to end, the whole header is needed for every packet of a flow, but over a single link much of it becomes redundant and can be left out, as long as the receiving end of the link can put it back transparently.

The header can be reduced by first sending the field information that is expected to stay static for the lifetime of the flow. Further compression comes from the fields that change more often, using methods chosen for the way each field is expected to change. To do this, the compressor and the decompressor each keep a context holding what they need from earlier packets. The two update their contexts on events that are not necessarily synchronised, so a loss or a damaged packet can leave the two out of step, which the document calls context damage. A robust scheme therefore needs both mechanisms to reduce the chance of context damage and mechanisms to repair it.
sections.plainLanguage: Every packet in a flow repeats the same addresses and the same options. On a single link those repeats are wasted bytes, so the sender can leave them out and the receiver can fill them in again from what it already knows.

sections.title: How Header Compression Got Here
sections.content:
The first header compression scheme, compressed TCP (CTCP), was introduced by Van Jacobson. Often called VJ compression, it compresses the 40 octets of the TCP/IP header down to 4 octets, and uses delta encoding for fields that change one after another. The compressor detects transport-level retransmissions and sends a header that updates the whole context when they occur, so the repair needs no explicit signalling between the two ends.

IP header compression, IPHC, improves on CTCP and can compress arbitrary IP, TCP and UDP headers. When compressing non-TCP headers it does not use delta encoding and is robust, and its repair mechanism is augmented with negative acknowledgements called CONTEXT_STATE messages, which speed up the repair but limit it by the round-trip time of the link. IPHC does not compress RTP headers.

CRTP is an RTP extension to IPHC. It compresses the 40 octets of IPv4, UDP and RTP headers to a minimum of 2 octets when the UDP checksum is not enabled, and to 4 octets when it is. On lossy links with long round-trip times CRTP does not perform well: each lost packet causes several later packets to fail to decompress, because the context stays invalid for at least one round-trip time, and the large headers sent to update the context waste bandwidth. Its local repair mechanism, TWICE, exploits the fact that when the flow of compressed packets is regular, the right guess after a lost packet is to apply the update twice. Even with TWICE, CRTP doubled the number of lost packets. The enhanced variant eCRTP was written to be more robust in the presence of reordering and loss, at the cost of extra overhead and so of lower compression efficiency.
sections.plainLanguage: Earlier schemes compressed well but were fragile: one lost packet could spoil several that followed. That is the problem ROHC was written to fix.

sections.title: Flows, Field Types and Contexts
sections.content:
The first step is to identify and group packets into flows, so that the redundancy from packet to packet is as large as possible. Grouping is usually based on the source and destination addresses, the transport protocol, the port numbers, and possibly extra application identifiers such as the synchronization source in RTP. The compressor and the decompressor each build a context for the flow and identify it with a Context Identifier carried in every compressed header.

The second step is to understand how each header field changes. Fields fall into classes. INFERRED fields can be worked out from other fields or from outside the packet, such as the frame size, which the link layer protocol can supply. STATIC fields are assumed constant for the lifetime of the flow, so their values are communicated only at the start. STATIC-DEF fields are the ones that define a flow, so packets that differ in them belong to different flows, and they are compressed as static fields. STATIC-KNOWN fields are expected to have well-known values and need not be communicated at all. CHANGING fields vary, either within a limited range or in some other manner, and are handled in more sophisticated ways.

The last step is to choose the encoding method for each field, and then to weigh compression efficiency against robustness to loss and errors and against the ability to detect errors in the decompression.
sections.plainLanguage: Before compressing anything, the two ends agree on what kind of traffic this is and what each field in the header is expected to do. A field that never changes is sent once; a field that the link can work out for itself is never sent at all.

sections.title: Efficiency, Robustness and Transparency
sections.content:
The performance of a header compression protocol is described with three parameters. Compression efficiency is how much the average header size is reduced. Robustness is the ability to tolerate packet losses, residual bit errors and out-of-order delivery on the link without losing additional packets or introducing additional errors in the decompressed headers. Compression transparency is the extent to which the scheme keeps the semantics of the original headers: if every decompressed header is bitwise identical to the original, the scheme is transparent.

The challenge is to reconcile all three. Increasing robustness always costs compression efficiency and the other way round, and the scheme has to be flexible enough to cope with the different round-trip times and loss patterns of the links where it is used. The scheme must give the decompressor a way to verify a decompression and detect possible context damage, and it must offer context recovery mechanisms such as feedback. The header compression schemes that came before the Robust Header Compression working group were not designed with these objectives in mind.
sections.plainLanguage: Three things matter at once: how small the header gets, how well the scheme survives a lossy link, and whether the rebuilt header is exactly right. You can have more of one only by giving up some of another.

sections.title: The ROHC Channel and Its Parameters
sections.content:
A ROHC channel is a logical unidirectional point-to-point channel carrying ROHC packets from one compressor to one decompressor, and it may carry feedback on behalf of another compressor-decompressor pair running the other way. Each compressed flow has a context, and each context has a Context Identifier. A context is new when the identifier is associated with a profile for the first time since the channel was created, or when it is associated with a different profile by an IR packet.

The identifier space is either small, with values from 0 to 15, or large, with values from 0 to 2^14 minus 1, which is 16383. Which of the two is used must be established, possibly by negotiation, before any compressed packet is sent. The space is distinct for each channel, so identifier 3 on one channel and identifier 3 on another do not refer to the same context even between the same nodes.

The channel also has a set of parameters agreed before the first packet. LARGE_CIDS is a boolean choosing the identifier representation. MAX_CID is the highest identifier the compressor will use, and by agreeing it the decompressor promises memory for at least that many contexts. PROFILES is the set of profiles both ends support, each identified by a 16-bit value whose lowest 8 bits give the profile and whose highest 8 bits give the variant, so only one variant of a profile may be in the set. FEEDBACK_FOR names the channel in the opposite direction that feedback on this channel refers to. MRRU is the maximum reconstructed reception unit, the largest reassembled unit in octets the decompressor is expected to build; if it is negotiated as zero, segmentation must not be used and received segments must be discarded.
sections.plainLanguage: Before any compressed packet is sent, the two ends agree on the rules: how many flows can share the link, which compression profiles are allowed, and how big a reassembled packet may be. A flow is identified by a short number carried in each packet.

sections.title: Packet Types and the General Format
sections.content:
A ROHC packet has up to four parts: any number of padding octets, any number of feedback elements, a header, and the payload. The header is either a profile-specific compressed header, an IR or IR-DYN header, or a segment. There can be at most one header in a packet, and it may be left out when the packet carries feedback only. At least one of feedback or header must be present.

Several packet types are reserved at the framework level: 11100000 for padding, 1110nnnn for an Add-CID octet where nnnn is an identifier from 1 to 15, 11110 for feedback, 11111000 for an IR-DYN packet, 1111110 for an IR packet, and 1111111 for a segment. The remaining patterns are available to individual profiles. A padding octet looks like an Add-CID octet for identifier 0, but must not be read as one.

Every header starts with a packet type indication, or with an Add-CID octet followed by the type indication. With a small identifier space, identifier 0 costs no bits at all and identifier 1 to 15 is written as an Add-CID octet. With a large identifier space the identifier is always present, in one or two octets. An IR header carries a one-octet profile identifier and an 8-bit CRC, and it associates the context with that profile and typically initialises the context. An IR-DYN header has the same shape but can never initialise a context that is not already initialised, though it can redefine which profile a context uses. The IR type octet is 1111110 and the IR-DYN type octet is 11111000.

The document also defines profile 0x0000, the uncompressed profile, which sends IP packets without compressing them. It is used when no compression profile is available for a packet or when compression is not wanted. After initialisation the only overhead is the size of the identifier, and a normal packet in this profile is an ordinary IP packet with identifier information attached.
sections.plainLanguage: Each packet names its type in the first bits. Some types set up a flow from scratch, some carry a compressed header, one carries feedback back the other way, and one is a piece of a packet too big to send at once.

sections.title: Feedback, Repair and Segmentation
sections.content:
Feedback carries information from the decompressor to the compressor. Three categories are defined. An ACK acknowledges successful decompression and says the decompressor considers its context valid. A NACK says the decompressor considers some or all of the dynamic part of its context invalid. A STATIC-NACK says the whole static context is invalid or was never established. Feedback can be interspersed, piggybacked on a data packet, or both. The length of a feedback element can be worked out from its first few octets, so a receiver can extract feedback without understanding it, and the identifier it carries says which context the feedback is about.

Checksums do the work of spotting errors. An 8-bit CRC in IR and IR-DYN headers covers at least the start of the header up to and including the profile field, and is enough to update the context safely when it verifies. A 3-bit CRC in a compressed header covers the whole original header and lets the decompressor check a decompression attempt, but it is too weak to be trusted on its own, so a profile should not allow a header with only a 3-bit CRC to be used to repair a context. A 7-bit CRC is strong enough to assume a repair worked from a single header, so a profile may allow decompression with it when part of the context is thought to be invalid. A 32-bit CRC protects the reassembled unit in the segmentation scheme.

ROHC also defines a simple segmentation protocol, for packets too large for the channel. It is not particularly efficient and is not meant to replace link-layer segmentation, and it assumes in-order delivery, using only a CRC and no sequence numbers, so it must not be used where in-order delivery cannot be guaranteed. Segments carry no identifier of their own and must arrive consecutively and in order; a final segment completes the reassembled unit, and if a non-segment packet follows a non-final segment the reassembly is aborted. A reassembled unit of 4 octets or less, one whose CRC fails, or one larger than the MRRU must be discarded.
sections.plainLanguage: Each compressed packet carries a small checksum. If the receiver rebuilds the header wrongly, the checksum will not match and it says so. A receiver can also send back a request to resend the parts of the context that have gone wrong.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Because encryption removes the redundancy that header compression schemes try to exploit, there is some inducement to forego encrypting headers in order to work over low-bandwidth links.

A malfunctioning or malicious header compressor could cause the decompressor to reconstitute packets that do not match the originals but still have valid headers, and possibly valid transport checksums as well. Such corruption may be detected with end-to-end authentication and integrity mechanisms, which compression does not affect. The ROHC scheme also uses an internal checksum to verify reconstructed headers, which reduces the chance of producing decompressed headers that do not match the originals without it being noticed.

Denial-of-service attacks are possible if an intruder can put bogus IR, IR-DYN or feedback packets onto the link and so reduce the compression efficiency. However, an intruder able to inject arbitrary packets at the link layer in this way raises additional security issues that dwarf those related to header compression.
sections.plainLanguage: Encrypting the header removes the very repetition that compression exploits, so there is a pull towards leaving it in the clear. The document also notes that a hostile compressor could hand the receiver a wrong header, and that a checksum is not the same as an end-to-end guarantee.

viz.caption: HOW A HEADER FIELD IS CLASSIFIED

items.title: INFERRED
items.text: Can be worked out from other fields or from outside the packet, such as the frame size, so it need not be sent.

items.title: STATIC
items.text: Assumed constant for the lifetime of the flow. The value is sent once.

items.title: STATIC-DEF
items.text: Defines the flow itself. Packets that differ in these fields belong to different flows.

items.title: STATIC-KNOWN
items.text: Expected to have a well-known value, so it need not be communicated at all.

items.title: CHANGING
items.text: Varies, and is handled with more careful encodings chosen for how it changes.

viz.caption: THE THREE PROPERTIES OF A COMPRESSION SCHEME

items.title: Compression efficiency
items.text: How much the average header is reduced by applying the scheme.

items.title: Robustness
items.text: Tolerating losses, residual bit errors and reordering without losing more packets or corrupting headers.

items.title: Compression transparency
items.text: Keeping the semantics of the original header. If every rebuilt header is bit for bit identical, the scheme is transparent.

layers.label: Feedback
layers.detail: Zero or more feedback elements for the compressor

layers.label: Header
layers.detail: A compressed header, an IR or IR-DYN header, or a segment

layers.label: Payload
layers.detail: The uncompressed payload that follows the last compressible header

viz.caption: THE PACKET TYPES RESERVED BY THE FRAMEWORK

items.label: Add-CID
items.desc: An Add-CID octet, where nnnn is an identifier from 1 to 15.

items.label: Feedback
items.desc: A feedback packet, which can carry variable-length feedback information.

items.label: Segment
items.desc: One segment of a packet that is too large for the channel.

items.title: 8-bit CRC
items.text: In IR and IR-DYN headers, covering at least the start of the header up to and including the profile field. Enough to update the context when it verifies.

items.title: 3-bit CRC
items.text: In compressed headers, covering the whole original header. Lets the decompressor check a decompression attempt, but is too weak to trust on its own.

items.title: 7-bit CRC
items.text: In compressed headers. Strong enough to assume a context repair worked from a single header.

items.title: 32-bit CRC
items.text: Used by the segmentation scheme to verify the reassembled unit.
